h1: Celeia hops for earthy lemon notes in pale lagers
title: Celeia Hops for Lemon in Pale Lager | Craft Beer School
desc: Celeia is a Slovenian aroma hop with floral, earthy and lemon notes. How to use it in a pale lager: timing, rates and a worked 1,000 litre plan.
teaser: A quiet hop for a clean lager. Celeia adds lemon and herbs without shouting over the malt.
standfirst: Celeia comes from the Styrian hop country of Slovenia and is grown for aroma. Its notes are floral, earthy and lemon, which suit a pale lager that has nowhere to hide. This guide covers where to add it and how much.
sections:
Celeia is a Slovenian aroma hop from the Savinja valley, the Styrian growing region around Žalec. It belongs with the gentle, European-style aroma hops. Alpha acids are low, roughly 3 to 6% depending on the crop, so it is not a bittering hop. You buy it for the oils.

The common descriptors are floral, herbal, earthy and a soft lemon note. It sits closer to a noble-style hop than to a fruity American variety. If you want grapefruit, look elsewhere. If you want a lager that smells fresh without tasting of one particular fruit, Celeia is a sensible choice.
Why a pale lager needs this kind of hop

A pale lager is a thin canvas. There is little malt sweetness or yeast ester to cover a harsh hop, so anything unpleasant shows. A soft aroma hop such as Celeia is forgiving at a modest rate.

It also pairs with low bitterness. Many pale lagers sit between 18 and 30 IBU. At that level the aroma has to carry the beer. A hop that adds lemon and herbs without grassiness gives it a lift and stops it turning into a pale ale.

Add the hop late and keep it cool. Hop oils are volatile, so a long boil removes the character you paid for. Take a 1,000 L pale lager at about 25 IBU. Use a high alpha hop at the start of the boil for the bitterness. Then add about 1 kg of Celeia (1 g per litre) in the whirlpool at 80 °C for 20 minutes. Keep another 500 g for a cold dry hop in the last days of lager fermentation.

Lager fermentation runs at 8 to 13 °C, cold enough to hold the oils in the beer. Dry hop at the cool end for two or three days. Skip the dry hop if the pellets are not fresh, because old pellets give hay instead of lemon.

A grassy edge appears when dry hopping runs long. Cold crash the tank after three days and taste daily. Floral notes arrive first and vegetal ones follow.

Keep oxygen out. Opening a tank to add hops lets air in unless you purge the port with CO2. Oxidised hop oils smell of cardboard and the lemon is the first note to go. If you have a dissolved oxygen meter, read it at packaging. A figure well under 100 parts per billion is a sensible target for a lager that has to last.

On the brewhouse floor, the usual failure is a whirlpool that is still too hot. Hop at 95 °C and you lose the lighter oils. Let the wort fall to 80 °C before the hops go in.

After primary fermentation, a pale lager rests warm for a day or two at about 14 to 16 °C so the yeast can clear diacetyl. Then it is cooled to 0 to 2 °C and held for two to four weeks. This is also when hop aroma settles into the beer.

Do not rush it. A lager that tastes rough at week one often tastes smooth at week three. The tank time is cheap compared with a batch that has to be explained to a customer. If your planning cannot afford the tank days, brew a golden ale with Celeia instead.

Celeia works alone, which is the clearest way to learn it. To build a blend, a small share of Loral adds floral lift. Palisade brings apricot and a green edge. For more orange, add a little Amarillo.

Keep the malt bill as pale as the style asks. Pilsner malt is the base, with rice or maize as a small share if you want a lighter body. Indian drinkers know that profile well. Our guide to brewing for India explains why adjuncts work in warm markets.
Buying and storing hops in India

Pellets travel better than whole cones. Keep them cold from the supplier to your cold room and buy for a few months at a time. Ask for the crop year and the alpha on the certificate of analysis. A lot that is two harvests old and has sat in a warm warehouse has lost its oils. The discount is not a bargain.

If you can only buy a small pack, use it all in one lager and keep the notes. A single clean trial teaches more than a half-used bag in a drawer.

Can I use Celeia in an ale?
Yes. It works well in pale ales, golden ales and saisons where you want a gentle, European-style hop rather than a fruity one.
